cards.title: Introduction to Java Operators
cards.content:
Operators in Java are special symbols used to perform operations on variables and values. Java provides a rich set of operators grouped into several categories:

  • Arithmetic Operators: Perform basic mathematical operations.
  • Unary Operators: Work with a single operand.
  • Relational & Logical Operators: Form conditions and evaluate truths.
  • Bitwise & Shift Operators: Manipulate individual bits of integer types.
  • Ternary & Assignment Operators: Simplify assignment and conditional evaluation.

cards.title: Arithmetic Operators in Depth
cards.content:
Java offers five core arithmetic operators: + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), / (division), and % (modulo).

Key considerations for Java developers:

  • Integer Division: Dividing two integers truncates the fractional part. E.g., 5 / 2 evaluates to 2.
  • Floating-point Division: To get a decimal value, at least one operand must be a float or double. E.g., 5.0 / 2 yields 2.5.
  • Modulo Operator: % returns the remainder of a division. It also works on negative numbers and floating-point types in Java.

content.question:
What will be the output of the following Java expression?

int result = 14 % 5 + 7 / 2;

cards.title: Unary Operators (Increment and Decrement)
cards.content:
Unary operators require only one operand. The most commonly used are the increment (++) and decrement (--) operators.

These can be applied in two ways:

  • Prefix (e.g., ++x): Increments the value first, then returns the newly incremented value.
  • Postfix (e.g., x++): Returns the original value first, then increments the variable behind the scenes.

cards.title: Relational and Logical Operators
cards.content:
Relational operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) compare operands and return a boolean.

Logical operators combine multiple boolean expressions:

  • && (Conditional-AND): Returns true if both conditions are true. Utilizes short-circuit evaluation.
  • || (Conditional-OR): Returns true if at least one condition is true. Utilizes short-circuit evaluation.
  • ! (Logical NOT): Reverses the boolean value.

Short-circuiting means that if the left hand side of an && evaluates to false, the right side is completely skipped, saving computing power and preventing runtime exceptions (like NullPointerExceptions).

content.question:
Consider the following statement. What happens when it is executed?

boolean result = (5 > 10) && (10 / 0 == 0);

options.text: It throws an ArithmeticException because of division by zero.
It compiles but fails to execute at runtime due to short-circuit evaluation.
It successfully evaluates to false without throwing any exception due to short-circuiting.

cards.title: Bitwise and Shift Operators
cards.content:
Java can manipulate integer types down to individual bits. These are critical for low-level systems programming, networking protocols, and performance-critical operations.

  • & (Bitwise AND): Performs AND on individual bits.
  • | (Bitwise OR): Performs OR on individual bits.
  • ^ (Bitwise XOR): Performs exclusive OR on bits.
  • ~ (Bitwise Complement): Inverts all bits (unary).
  • << (Left shift): Shifts bits to the left, filling empty spaces with 0.
  • >> (Signed right shift): Shifts bits right, preserving the sign bit.
  • >>> (Unsigned right shift): Shifts bits right, padding the left with 0s.

cards.title: Ternary and Compound Assignment Operators
cards.content:
The ternary operator (? :) is a shorthand for an if-else statement that returns a value: 

int min = (a < b) ? a : b;

Compound assignment operators combine an arithmetic/bitwise operator with an assignment (e.g., +=, *=, &=).

Pro-Tip: Compound assignments perform an implicit typecast. For instance, short s = 5; s += 2; compiles successfully, while s = s + 2; fails compilation because s + 2 evaluates to an int.

cards.title: Operator Best Practices & Summary
cards.content:
Writing high-quality Java code requires mastering operator side-effects and ensuring code clarity:

  • Use Parentheses: Even if you know operator precedence by heart, use parentheses to clarify intent. (a && b) || c is much easier to digest than a && b || c.
  • Avoid Side-Effects in Expressions: Writing statements like a[++i] = i++; causes undefined behavior/confusion. Separate incremental steps from standard evaluations.
  • Beware of Overflow: Operators in Java do not throw exceptions when numeric limits are exceeded. Multiplying large ints can silently wrap around to negative numbers.
